checks.claim: Cooking is the leading cause of reported US home fires, roughly 44 to 49 percent depending on the NFPA report (44 percent in 2017–2021 data).
checks.why: The notes support cooking as the leading cause. The NFPA cooking report gives 44 percent and a Fire Prevention Week 2023 release gives 49 percent, so 'about half' is only loosely true.

sources.title: Cooking Fires are the Leading Cause of Home Fires - 90.7 WKGC Public Media

checks.claim: Utilities add mercaptan, a chemical that smells like rotten eggs, to odorless natural gas so leaks are noticed.
checks.why: FortisBC, the GAO and WFAA all support this: natural gas is odorless and mercaptan is added so leaks can be detected.

sources.title: What does natural gas smell like?
GAS PIPELINE SAFETY Stakeholders' and Officials' Views on Federal Odorizing
Why does natural gas smell like rotten eggs?

checks.claim: A natural gas flame has a theoretical maximum (adiabatic) flame temperature of about 1,960 °C in air; real stove flames are usually cooler.
checks.why: Engineering ToolBox gives 1960 °C and Wikipedia gives 1,963 °C for methane in air. These are theoretical values, so 'about 1950' is close but not the sourced figure.

checks.claim: James Sharp, an Englishman, patented a gas stove in Northampton in 1826 and opened a gas stove factory in 1836.
checks.why: Wikipedia's Gas stove article gives both dates and the Northampton location. A timeline source confirms the 1826 patent. The script should not call it the 'first' gas stove, since Winzler's 1802 stove came earlier.
